text: Time to put the whole chapter to work in one real task. You've got a small list representing open tickets, and the job is to find exactly the ones a team lead would want to see first thing in the morning.

Five tickets, each an object with a number, a priority, and whether it's already assigned. Before writing any code, trace through by hand which ones should end up in the final answer: priority one and unassigned only describes the first ticket and the last one. Knowing that answer ahead of time is what lets you catch a mistake instead of just trusting whatever the code produces.

Filter walks the array and keeps only the tickets where the function returns true. The condition here uses the logical AND operator to require two things at once: priority strictly equals one, and assigned strictly equals false. Both comparisons use triple equals on purpose, avoiding any type coercion. At this point, the result of filter is still an array of full ticket objects - nothing has been reshaped yet.

Map takes that filtered array and builds a new one, pulling out just the number property from each remaining ticket. Run the whole thing, and the result is exactly the two ticket numbers from the original trace - confirming the logic actually matches what you expected by hand.

Notice everything this chapter covered showed up in one function: object properties for priority and assigned, the strict equality and AND operators for the condition, and filter followed by map for narrowing the list down and then reshaping what's left. That filter-then-map pattern is one you will use constantly.

Variables, operators, functions, arrays, objects - the whole foundation is in place. Next up: Chapter 2 begins, starting with ServiceNow's own server-side JavaScript engine, where this exact language starts running inside the platform itself.
